evidence_cards.title: MEPS 2016: people with a reported ICD-10 A69 (other spirochetal infections, which includes Lyme disease)
evidence_cards.definition: People with at least one condition record whose 3-character ICD10CDX equals A69.
evidence_cards.method: Sum of unique-person weights (PERWT16F) over the domain; standard error by Taylor linearisation over VARSTR/VARPSU. Person-level, one year only.
comparability: A69 is the broad category that contains Lyme (A69.2x); MEPS public files keep only the first 3 characters, so this is NOT a Lyme-specific count and must not be read as Lyme prevalence.
MEPS panels overlap across adjacent years: never add or pool these yearly totals.
Condition rows come from household reports coded by professional coders.

AHRQ (MEPS team, 2026-09-24) urges caution forming Lyme cost estimates from MEPS: pooling 2016-2024 gives only about 300-400 observations, expenditures are highly skewed (about 1,000 or more are needed for a solid mean), only treated Lyme is identified (zero-expenditure cases drop out, biasing upward), events may be flagged as arthritis without naming Lyme, comorbidities cannot be separated from Lyme, and onset dates are not recorded. Lyme-specific A69.2 is available only in restricted data centers.

uncertainty.note: Small samples give very wide, unreliable intervals.

evidence_cards.summary: 2016: about 436,208 people (95% CI 250,739 to 621,678; 31 sampled persons) reported a condition coded A69.
evidence_cards.how_to_use: Cross-check or population context only, never a prevalence of Lyme or Long COVID; not a cost estimate (events are counts, not dollars).

contextual_issues: Caregiver/family strain is referenced ('Diminished work performance exacts a toll on the worker, the worker's family and the employer') but not measured or quantified by this study.
Insurance denials and out-of-network care are discussed as a likely driver of higher out-of-pocket costs but are not separately quantified.

The document cites, without adopting as its own measurement, an external estimate that 'as many as 36%' of early-treated Lyme patients remain ill after treatment (Aucott et al., 2013) and that 20-45% report fatigue/pain/sleep disturbance six months later (Aucott et al., 2013) - these are background citations, not this study's own findings.

The document cites (not as its own finding) that chronic illness accounts for 84% of healthcare costs (Anderson, 2010) and that ~80% of chronic-illness cost is productivity loss (Devol & Bedroussian, 2007) - general chronic-disease literature, not Lyme-specific or this study's own estimate.

The document notes (citing Fallon et al., 2008) that one NIH-funded trial screened 3,368 patients to enroll only 36 meeting restrictive entry criteria, illustrating research-recruitment difficulty, but this is an external study's result, not this paper's own data.
evidence_gaps: No total or aggregate dollar cost of Lyme disease/CLD (national or per-patient medical expenditure) was calculated; the authors state explicitly that 'this study was not designed to measure total medical expenditures.'
No dollar value for lost productivity/income was calculated; the authors state 'it is beyond the scope of this study to calculate the economic cost of this loss of productivity.'
No caregiver time or caregiver-cost data were collected.
No quantification of insurance-denial rates or amounts, despite being discussed as a likely cost driver.

No breakdown of cost, utilization, or employment-impact figures by sex, age group, race/ethnicity, disability status, veteran status, or geographic region beyond four broad US census regions (no regional cost/utilization breakdown given).
No lifetime-cost extrapolation is possible from this data; figures describe a single preceding-year snapshot for a sample restricted to symptoms persisting ≥6 months post-treatment.
comparison_boundaries: Out-of-pocket cost percentages differ between the Results section (43% of CLD patients >$5,000; general population 6%) and the Discussion section (46%; general population 5%) for what appears to be the same quantity; these two internally inconsistent figures should not be averaged or silently reconciled - report both with their respective locators.

Table 4 subgroup percentages for >$5,000 out-of-pocket costs (37.3% EM rash/serology-diagnosed vs. 46.4% other-laboratory-diagnosed, full sample 43.2%) are a different stratification than the headline 43%/46% figures above and should not be pooled across these groupings without noting the diagnostic-basis split.

'Stopped working' and 'reduced hours/changed role' percentages are stated slightly differently in main text (42%, 25%) versus Table 4 (41.3%, 29.2%); treat as two reportings of a related but not identical statistic rather than a single number.

The CLD sample is a self-selected, internet-recruited convenience sample (not randomly drawn, skews 82.6% female, slightly older than general population); its utilization/cost/employment figures cannot be pooled with population-representative surveillance or claims data as if drawn from the same sampling frame.

The CDC's 300,000/year estimate (adopted from CDC-funded studies using self-reported diagnosis, insurance coding, and positive serology) and the prior ~30,000/year surveillance count are different measurement methods with different case definitions and time windows; the document itself states only that 'the surveillance system does not reflect the full spectrum of the disease seen clinically' and that 'the difference between those counted as cases and the 270,000+ who are not is unknown' - do not characterize either number as 'the true incidence' or assign a specific proportion of the gap to under-reporting versus over-diagnosis, as the document does not do so itself.

Out-of-pocket cost and utilization figures refer to 'the preceding year' relative to an early-2013 survey administration (~2012-2013); no standardized price year is stated, so these figures should not be treated as inflation-indexed to a specific calendar year for cross-study comparison.

claims_undercounting_caveat.basis: The document states that CDC's revised ~300,000/year estimate arose from 'preliminary review of three CDC funded studies that did not utilize the restrictive CDC surveillance criteria, but rather relied on self-reported diagnosis, insurance coding by healthcare providers, and positive serology' (p.14-15) - i.e., the modeled estimate is partly grounded in insurance/diagnosis-coding data, distinct from the narrower surveillance-case count.

subgroup_disaggregation_caveat.pooled_value: All cost, utilization, and employment-impact figures (e.g., the >$2,000/>$5,000 out-of-pocket percentages, doctor/ER/hospital/homecare utilization rates, and employment/disability percentages) are reported as single pooled statistics for the full CLD working sample (82.6% female, mean age 48.2) with no breakdown by sex, age group, race/ethnicity, disability status, or other subgroup, despite the sample's own demographic skew.

systemic_gap_caveat.description: The document describes an insurance-coverage/regulatory gap: many insurers have adopted restrictive Lyme disease treatment guidelines and may decline to cover extended antibiotic therapy or other medications commonly used for CLD, pushing patients toward out-of-network, higher-out-of-pocket care.
systemic_gap_caveat.basis: Discussion, p.13-14: 'it is likely that these physician visits would be out of network because many insurers have adopted restrictive Lyme disease guidelines and may not cover extended therapy with antibiotics or other medications often used for CLD treatment.'

decision_relevance.summary: A simulator built on this document could help patients/advocates and clinicians anticipate the relative scale of out-of-pocket costs, healthcare utilization, and work/employment impact associated with persistent post-treatment Lyme symptoms, benchmarked against general-population reference data the authors cite. Payers/policy audiences could use the utilization and out-of-pocket figures to motivate discussion of insurance coverage restrictions for extended Lyme treatment and the potential value of earlier diagnosis. Because the sample is a self-selected, non-representative internet cohort and the study explicitly did not calculate total medical expenditures or a productivity-loss dollar figure, any simulator must present these as patient-reported relative-burden indicators from a convenience sample, not as validated population-level cost estimates.
use_cases: Patients/advocates could compare their own reported symptom burden, utilization pattern, or out-of-pocket spending against this cohort's reported ranges (e.g., 69% exceeding $2,000, 43-46% exceeding $5,000 out-of-pocket per year) to contextualize their own experience, with clear labeling that this is a non-representative patient-survey sample, not a population estimate.

Policy/payer users could use the utilization-ratio findings (e.g., ~5x more doctor visits, ~6x more homecare visits than general population) alongside the document's note on restrictive insurer coverage of extended antibiotic therapy to inform discussion of coverage policy gaps for post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome, without treating the figures as a national cost total.

## Source and sample
Figures come from Johnson et al. (2014, PeerJ), a survey of 3,090 self-selected, internet-recruited respondents clinically diagnosed with Lyme disease whose symptoms persisted more than six months after antibiotic treatment ('chronic Lyme disease,' CLD). The sample is 82.6% female with a mean age of 48.2 and is not drawn randomly from the population, so figures describe this specific convenience sample, not a population estimate. Survey administration was in early 2013, describing the preceding year; out-of-pocket dollar thresholds are in 2013 dollars.

## What is and is not modeled
The simulator reproduces patient-reported percentages for out-of-pocket spending thresholds, doctor-visit frequency, and employment, benchmarked against general-population reference figures the authors cite from NHIS, NAMCS/NHAMCS, and BLS. It does not compute a total dollar cost of Lyme disease or a dollar value of lost productivity: the authors state explicitly that the study was not designed to measure total medical expenditures and that calculating productivity-loss costs was beyond its scope. Caregiver time and insurance-denial amounts were not collected and are not modeled.

## Limitations to keep in view
The out-of-pocket and employment figures are reported only as single pooled statistics for the full sample, with no breakdown by sex, age group, race/ethnicity, or disability status, despite the sample's own demographic skew; federal survey data such as NHIS and BRFSS generally supports disaggregated analysis even though this document did not perform one here. The document also discusses the CDC's estimate that roughly 300,000 people are diagnosed with Lyme disease annually, a figure partly derived from insurance coding and self-reported diagnosis rather than the narrower surveillance case definition used for the prior ~30,000/year count; the authors state the system 'does not reflect the full spectrum of the disease seen clinically' but do not attribute the gap to a specific cause, so this estimate should not be treated as a complete or fully validated count. Separately, the document notes that many insurers have adopted restrictive Lyme treatment guidelines that may not cover extended antibiotic or other CLD-directed therapy, which the authors suggest pushes patients toward out-of-network, higher out-of-pocket care - a gap in coverage policy, distinct from the accuracy of the burden figures themselves. Finally, the Results section (43%, comparator 6%) and Discussion section (46%, comparator 5%) report slightly different values for the same >$5,000/year out-of-pocket statistic; both are reported above without being averaged or reconciled.

## Federal cross-check (computed by the system, not by the AI model)

The model only read these quantities from the document; the comparisons below were calculated in code from federal data files. The federal figures are published or surveyed values; the simulator's own outputs are modeled from the uploaded document.

- Out-of-pocket Lyme-related expense threshold: $2,000/year: 2,000.00 in 2013 dollars is about 2,763.97 in 2025 dollars (CPI-U all items, x1.382). This is general price inflation, not medical-care inflation, and is a restatement, not a measurement. Federal source: published price index, 1913-2025; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
- Out-of-pocket Lyme-related expense threshold: $5,000/year: 5,000.00 in 2013 dollars is about 6,909.92 in 2025 dollars (CPI-U all items, x1.382). This is general price inflation, not medical-care inflation, and is a restatement, not a measurement. Federal source: published price index, 1913-2025; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
- CDC's 2013 estimate of annually diagnosed Lyme disease cases in the US (2013, the United States): the document's estimate of 300,000 is 8.3 times the 36,307 cases CDC received as reported. Reported cases are a passive-surveillance subset, so estimates from claims or models are usually higher; this shows the size of the gap, not which figure is right. Federal source: public health surveillance (surveillance report), 2008-2021; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
